extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners; patent practitioners and applicants
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating patent claims for subject-matter eligibility under the July 2015 USPTO Interim Eligibility Guidance (Alice/Mayo framework), including how to identify judicial exceptions and evaluate whether additional claim elements amount to 'significantly more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima Facie Case of Eligibility (examiner burden)
rubrics_metrics.description: A prima facie case of eligibility requires the examiner to explain why a claim or claims are unpatentable clearly and specifically, so that applicant has sufficient notice and is able to effectively respond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner’s burden is met by clearly articulating the reason(s) why the claimed invention is not eligible, for example by providing a reasoned rationale that identifies the judicial exception recited in the claim and why it is considered an exception, and that identifies the additional elements in the claim (if any) and explains why they do not amount to significantly more than the exception. This rationale may rely, where appropriate, on the knowledge generally available to those in the art, on the case law precedent, on applicant’s own disclosure, or on evidence. Sample rejections satisfying this burden are found in the training materials (worksheets for Examples 5–8).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify the judicial exception recited in the claim and explain why it is an exception
rubrics_metrics.description: When asserting a claim is directed to a judicial exception, the examiner must identify which exception is implicated by the claim language and explain why that concept is an exception under controlling case law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a reasoned rationale that identifies the judicial exception recited in the claim and why it is considered an exception; tie the claimed concept to judicial descriptors or court-identified abstract ideas rather than labeling without explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify claim additional elements and evaluate 'significantly more'
rubrics_metrics.description: For claims that recite a judicial exception plus additional elements, examiners must identify those additional elements and explain why they do or do not amount to 'significantly more' than the judicial exception itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Supreme Court and Federal Circuit considerations (illustrated in Examples 21–25) to determine whether the additional elements integrate the exception into a practical application or otherwise add an inventive concept. Explain reasoning clearly so applicant can respond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of case law, training materials, applicant disclosure, or evidence to support rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners may base their eligibility rationale on knowledge generally available to those in the art, judicial precedent, the applicant’s own disclosure, or other evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite relevant case law (see Appendix 3 index), refer to training worksheets and examples (Appendix 1 and training materials), and where appropriate, point to applicant disclosure or proffered evidence to substantiate why a claim element is well-understood, routine, or conventional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply streamlined analysis when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: The July 2015 Update identifies a 'streamlined' analysis path and provides examples (26 & 27) illustrating its application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use streamlined analysis in cases where the claim clearly is not directed to a judicial exception or where other simplifications are appropriate per the Update; consult Examples 26 & 27 for illustration of situations where the streamlined approach applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine when a claim is not directed to any judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Part of the eligibility determination is concluding that a claim is not directed to a judicial exception; Examples 23 & 27 illustrate claims found not directed to any judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim, when properly assessed, is not similar to court-identified exceptions or otherwise does not recite an exception, then eligibility can be found without further Alice-step analysis. Explain why the claim is not directed to an exception with reference to claim language and examples/case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify abstract ideas using judicial descriptors in Step 2A
rubrics_metrics.description: Section III and the graphic associate concepts held to be abstract ideas in court decisions with judicial descriptors (e.g., 'certain methods of organizing human activities'), to guide examiners in identifying abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claimed concept should not be identified as an abstract idea unless it is similar to at least one concept that the courts have identified as an abstract idea. Use the descriptor categories and concrete examples from the Update to map claim concepts to court-identified abstract ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental Economic Practices (abstract-idea descriptor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concepts relating to the economy and commerce, such as agreements between people in the form of contracts, legal obligations, and business relations (labeled 'Fundamental Economic Practices').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include creating a contractual relationship, hedging, mitigating settlement risk, processing loan information, tax-free investing, and displaying an advertisement in exchange for access to copyrighted media. Use these examples when assessing whether a claim recites a fundamental economic practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: An Idea 'Of Itself' (abstract-idea descriptor)
rubrics_metrics.description: An idea standing alone such as an uninstantiated concept, plan or scheme, as well as a mental process that 'can be performed in the human mind, or by a human using a pen and paper.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include obtaining and comparing intangible data, data recognition and storage, organizing information to store and transmit, diagnosing by performing clinical tests and thinking about results, and other purely mental processes. Assess whether the claim merely recites an uninstantiated idea or mental process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certain Methods of Organizing Human Activity (abstract-idea descriptor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concepts relating to interpersonal and intrapersonal activities such as managing relationships or transactions between people, social activities, advertising/marketing/sales, and managing human mental activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include structuring a sales force or marketing company, managing an insurance policy, managing a game of bingo, meal planning, and other organizational/practical human-activity methods. Use these examples to evaluate whether a claim's concept fits this descriptor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical Relationships/Formulas (abstract-idea descriptor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical concepts such as algorithms, mathematical relationships, mathematical formulas, and calculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include an algorithm for converting binary coded decimal to pure binary, formulas for computing alarm limits, formulas describing electromagnetic phenomena, Arrhenius equation, algorithms for computing prices and financial analyses, and calculating differences between local and average data values. Determine whether the claim's core is a mathematical concept and evaluate integration into practical application or additional elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use indexes of examples and eligibility cases as evaluative resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Appendix 1 provides new illustrative examples; Appendix 2 is an index of examples (subject matter, statutory category, judicial exception, relevant considerations); Appendix 3 lists eligibility cases from the Supreme Court and Federal Circuit with citation and classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult the indexed examples and case summaries to inform determinations, identify analogous situations, and support reasoned rationales. The indexes are intended to be used as references for consistent application of the guidance.
